claim: Myomatrix arrays are a novel class of electrode devices that record muscle activity at unprecedented resolution across muscles and behaviors.
source: Here we present a novel class of electrode devices ('Myomatrix arrays') that record muscle activity at unprecedented resolution across muscles and behaviors.
evidence: This is a primary claim stated directly in the abstract describing the main contribution of the work.

claim: High-density, flexible electrode arrays allow for stable recordings from motor units during natural behaviors in many species, including mice, rats, primates, songbirds, frogs, and insects.
source: High-density, flexible electrode arrays allow for stable recordings from the muscle fibers activated by a single motor neuron, called a 'motor unit,' during natural behaviors in many species, including mice, rats, primates, songbirds, frogs, and insects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple species shown throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1-3.

claim: Current methods for recording muscle fiber activity via electromyography can resolve the activity of individual motor units in only a limited range of settings.
source: However, our understanding of motor unit activity during natural behaviors is rudimentary due to the difficulty of recording spike trains from motor unit populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and comparison data showing limitations of traditional EMG methods.

claim: Traditional EMG methods require that a subject's movements be highly restricted, typically in isometric force tasks, to prevent measurement artifacts.
source: First, to prevent measurement artifacts, traditional EMG methods require that a subject's movements be highly restricted, typically in 'isometric' force tasks where subjects contract their muscles without moving their bodies (Bräcklein et al., 2022; Farina and Holobar, 2016; Marshall et al., 2022; Negro et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature describing limitations of traditional EMG.

claim: Fine-wire electrodes typically cannot detect single motor unit activity in small muscles, including the muscles of mice or songbirds.
source: Moreover, fine-wire electrodes typically cannot detect single motor unit activity in small muscles, including the muscles of widely used model systems such as mice or songbirds (Pearson et al., 2005; Srivastava et al., 2015; Pack et al., 2023), and surface electrode arrays are poorly tolerated by freely behaving animal subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is contrasted with Myomatrix performance data.

claim: Each motor neuron's action potential reliably evokes a single spike in its target muscle fibers.
source: Because each action potential in a motor neuron reliably evokes a single spike in its target muscle fibers, action potentials recorded from muscle provide a high-resolution readout of motor neuron activity in the spinal cord and brainstem.
evidence: This is established neuroscience knowledge about motor unit physiology.

claim: Myomatrix arrays were fabricated using layers of polyimide and gold deposited on a carrier wafer.
source: Layers of insulating polymer (polyimide) and conductive metal (gold) are successively deposited on a carrier wafer to form a flexible, 20- or 40-μm-thick electrode array of gold electrode contacts, which receive a surface treatment of PEDOT to improve recording properties (see 'Methods').
evidence: This claim describes the fabrication process shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and detailed in Methods.

claim: Myomatrix arrays have a thickness of 20 or 40 micrometers.
source: The final device thickness was ~40 µm for the injectable (primate forelimb) design and ~20 µm for all other design variants.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the Methods section.

claim: Electrode contacts on Myomatrix arrays are coated with PEDOT:PSS to reduce electrode impedance.
source: Electrode sites are then coated with a conductive polymer, PEDOT:PSS (Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-poly(styrene-sulfonate)), (Cui and Martin, 2003; Dijk et al., 2020; Rossetti et al., 2019) to reduce the electrode impedance (Ludwig et al., 2011).
evidence: This fabrication detail is supported by citations to prior work on PEDOT:PSS properties.

claim: PEDOT:PSS coating resulted in final electrode impedances of 5 kOhm or less for 100 × 200 μm electrode sites.
source: PEDOT:PSS was deposited on the electrode contacts to a thickness of 100 nm using spin coating, resulting in final electrode impedances of 5 kOhm or less (100 × 200 um electrode sites).
evidence: This is a direct measurement of electrode impedance after PEDOT:PSS coating.

claim: Myomatrix arrays can isolate individual motor units during mouse locomotion.
source: Single motor units were routinely isolated during mouse locomotion in our Myomatrix recordings (Figure 1), but never in the fine-wire datasets from Miri et al., 2017 we reanalyzed or, to our knowledge, in any prior study.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and comparison with fine-wire EMG data.

claim: Fine-wire EMG did not isolate any individual motor units during mouse locomotion in reanalyzed datasets from Miri et al., 2017.
source: Single motor units were routinely isolated during mouse locomotion in our Myomatrix recordings (Figure 1), but never in the fine-wire datasets from Miri et al., 2017 we reanalyzed or, to our knowledge, in any prior study.
evidence: This claim is based on reanalysis of published data using the same spike-sorting methods applied to Myomatrix data.

claim: Myomatrix arrays have significantly higher signal-to-noise ratios than fine-wire EMG arrays in multiunit recordings.
source: Moreover, in multiunit recordings, Myomatrix arrays have significantly higher signal-to-noise ratios than fine-wire EMG arrays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claim: SNR values from Myomatrix arrays are significantly greater than those from fine-wire EMG when all data are pooled (p=0.002).
source: SNR values from Myomatrix arrays are significantly greater than those from fine-wire EMG, both when all data shown in (d) are pooled and when only data from day 14 are included (two-sample KS-test, p=0.002 and 0.038, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical test result comparing SNR measurements between Myomatrix and fine-wire EMG.

claim: At least four Myomatrix threads bearing a total of 32 electrodes can be inserted into one mouse muscle.
source: In contrast, at least four Myomatrix 'threads' (Figure 1a), bearing a total of 32 electrodes, can be inserted into one muscle (Figure 1c shows 5 of 32 channels recorded simultaneously from mouse triceps), greatly expanding the number of recording channels within a single muscle.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Traditional fine-wire EMG typically provides only a single bipolar recording channel per mouse muscle.
source: Second, because wire-based EMG requires inserting an additional wire for each additional electrode contact, only a single pair of wires (providing a single bipolar recording channel, Figure 1b, bottom) can be inserted into an individual mouse muscle in most cases (Miri et al., 2017; Tysseling et al., 2013; Tysseling et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim about limitations of fine-wire EMG is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Myomatrix arrays recorded isolated motor units for up to 4791 stride cycles in mice during continuous recording sessions lasting 10-60 minutes.
source: In triceps recordings during locomotion in rodents (Figures 1 and 2c), isolated motor units were recorded for up to 4791 stride cycles (mice) or 491 stride cycles (rats) during continuous recording sessions lasting 10–60 min.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of recording stability during behavior.

claim: Individual motor units were most frequently recorded in the first 2 weeks of chronic recordings.
source: Although individual motor units were most frequently recorded in the first 2 wk of chronic recordings (see main text), Myomatrix arrays also isolate individual motor units after much longer periods of chronic implantation, as shown here where spikes from two individual motor units (colored boxes in bottom trace) were isolated during locomotion 65 d after implantation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e and discussed in the main text.

claim: Myomatrix arrays isolated individual motor units during locomotion 65 days after implantation.
source: Although individual motor units were most frequently recorded in the first 2 wk of chronic recordings (see main text), Myomatrix arrays also isolate individual motor units after much longer periods of chronic implantation, as shown here where spikes from two individual motor units (colored boxes in bottom trace) were isolated during locomotion 65 d after implantation.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the example recording shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e.

claim: Myomatrix recordings in nonhuman primates maintained single-unit isolation across 1292 reaching trials collected over 97 minutes.
source: Myomatrix recordings in behaving nonhuman primates were similarly long-lived, as in the dataset shown in Figure 3, where single-unit isolation was maintained across 1292 reaching trials collected over 97 min.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of recording stability in primates shown in Figure 3.

claim: The duration of single-unit EMG recording was limited by the willingness of the animal to continue performing the behavior, rather than a loss of signal isolation.
source: In each of these datasets, the duration of single-unit EMG recording was limited by the willingness of the animal to continue performing the behavior, rather than a loss of signal isolation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that recordings remained stable until behavioral sessions ended.

claim: Myomatrix arrays did not show voltage artifacts at any point in the stride cycle during rodent locomotion recordings.
source: In recordings from rodents during locomotion (Figures 1b and 2c), we did not observe voltage artifacts at any point in the stride cycle (e.g. when the paw of the recorded limb first touches the ground in each stride cycle; Figure 2c, black arrowhead).
evidence: This observation is based on examination of the recorded data during locomotion.

claim: Movement artifacts were absent during active arm movements in monkeys with peak fingertip speeds of approximately 15 cm/s and peak elbow angle velocity of approximately 40°/s.
source: Movement artifacts were similarly absent during active arm movements in monkeys (peak fingertip speeds ~15 cm/s; peak elbow angle velocity ~40°/s, Figure 3b and e), during passive jaw displacement in anesthetized mice (Figure 2b), or in the other anesthetized preparations shown in Figure 2.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of recordings during movements with measured kinematics.

claim: Injectable Myomatrix arrays yielded motor unit recordings during arm movements in rhesus macaques.
source: As shown in Figure 3a–d, injectable Myomatrix arrays yielded motor unit recordings during arm movements.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Thirteen motor units were recorded simultaneously during a single trial in which a monkey reached to a target.
source: Tick marks in Figure 3d show the activity of 13 motor units recorded simultaneously during a single trial in which a monkey was cued (by a force perturbation which causes an extension of the elbow joint) to reach to a target.
evidence: This is a direct count of motor units isolated from the data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Conventional fine-wire EMG inserted into the same muscle as Myomatrix arrays yielded only a single trace reflecting the activity of an unknown number of motor units.
source: In contrast to the ensemble of motor units recorded with a Myomatrix probe, conventional fine-wire EMGs inserted into the same muscle (in a separate recording session) yielded only a single trace reflecting the activity of an unknown number of motor units (Figure 3e, middle).
evidence: This comparison is based on data from the same muscle in the same animal but different recording sessions.

claim: Polyimide was selected as a substrate material due to its strength and flexibility and the ease with which sub-millimeter features could be defined.
source: We selected polyimide as a substrate material due to its strength and flexibility and the ease with which we could define electrode contacts, suture holes, and other sub-millimeter features that facilitate implantation and recording stability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: This is a design rationale based on material properties.

claim: The fabrication pipeline allows rapid development and refinement of multiple array designs.
source: This fabrication pipeline allows the rapid development and refinement of multiple array designs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the variety of designs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myomatrix arrays can record from forelimb, hindlimb, orofacial, pelvic, vocal, and respiratory muscles.
source: Below, we show how Myomatrix arrays provide high-resolution measurements of motor unit activation in a variety of species and muscle groups including forelimb, hindlimb, orofacial, pelvic, vocal, and respiratory muscles.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Myomatrix recordings isolated motor units from the mouse triceps during a head-fixed pellet reaching task.
source: Beyond the locomotor and postural signals shown in Figure 1, Myomatrix recordings from mouse triceps also provided single-unit EMG data during a head-fixed reaching task (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Myomatrix arrays recorded single motor unit EMG data from the mouse superficial masseter muscle during reflexive muscle contraction evoked by passive jaw displacement.
source: Figure 2b shows single motor unit EMG data recorded from the superficial masseter (jaw) muscle when reflexive muscle contraction was obtained by passively displacing the jaw of an anesthetized mouse.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained isolated motor units from rat triceps during locomotion.
source: To extend these methods across species, we collected Myomatrix recordings from muscles of the rat forelimb, obtaining isolated motor units from the triceps during locomotion (Figure 2c) and a digit-flexing muscle in the lower forearm during head-free reaching (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Myomatrix arrays can isolate motor unit waveforms evoked by direct optogenetic stimulation of spinal motor neurons.
source: Myomatrix arrays can furthermore isolate motor unit waveforms evoked by direct optogenetic stimulation of spinal motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the spinal cord evokes spiking in single motor units with millisecond-scale timing jitter.
source: Figure 2e shows recordings of light-evoked spikes in the mouse bulbospongiosus muscle (BSM, a pelvic muscle that wraps around the base of the penis in male mice), demonstrating that optogenetic stimulation of the spinal cord evokes spiking in single motor units with millisecond-scale timing jitter (Figure 2e, center) and with latencies (Figure 2e, right) consistent with the latencies of recordings obtained with fine-wire electrodes (Lenschow et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of optogenetically evoked responses shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Optogenetically evoked motor unit spikes have latencies between 10 and 15 ms, consistent with results obtained from traditional fine-wire electrodes in mice.
source: Figure 2e shows recordings of light-evoked spikes in the mouse bulbospongiosus muscle (BSM, a pelvic muscle that wraps around the base of the penis in male mice), demonstrating that optogenetic stimulation of the spinal cord evokes spiking in single motor units with millisecond-scale timing jitter (Figure 2e, center) and with latencies (Figure 2e, right) consistent with the latencies of recordings obtained with fine-wire electrodes (Lenschow et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim compares Myomatrix measurements with prior fine-wire EMG results.

claim: Simple modifications of the basic electrode array design allowed high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats.
source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained high-resolution recordings from vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds.
source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2g and h.

claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained high-resolution recordings from body wall muscles in moth larvae.
source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Myomatrix arrays obtained high-resolution recordings from leg muscles in frogs.
source: Beyond rodents, simple modifications of the basic electrode array design (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) allowed us to obtain high-resolution recordings from hindlimb muscles in cats (Figure 2f), vocal and respiratory muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g and h, see also Zia et al., 2020), body wall muscles in moth larvae (Figure 2i), and leg muscles in frogs (Figure 2j).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: The mouse lateral head of the triceps muscle is approximately 9 mm in length with a mass of 0.02 g.
source: These methods allow the user to record simultaneously from ensembles of single motor units (Figure 1c and d) in freely behaving animals, even from small muscles including the lateral head of the triceps muscle in mice (approximately 9 mm in length with a mass of 0.02 g; Mathewson et al., 2012).
evidence: This anatomical measurement is cited from prior literature.

claim: In songbird vocal muscles, most individual motor neurons innervate only 1-3 muscle fibers.
source: These approaches will be particularly valuable in muscles in which each motor neuron controls a very small number of muscle fibers, allowing fine control of oculomotor muscles in mammals as well as vocal muscles in songbirds (Figure 2g), in which most individual motor neurons innervate only 1–3 muscle fibers (Adam et al., 2021).
evidence: This anatomical fact about songbird vocal muscles is cited from prior literature.

claim: Motor unit action potential waveforms from individual motor units were identified using analysis methods previously used to sort spikes from neural data.
source: Motor unit action potential waveforms from individual motor units were identified with analysis methods previously used to sort spikes from neural data.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used to process Myomatrix data.

claim: Myomatrix signals were band-passed between 350 and 7000 Hz.
source: In all cases, Myomatrix signals (sampling rate 30 or 40 kHz) were first band-passed between 350 and 7000 Hz.
evidence: This is a data processing parameter used in the analysis.

claim: Kilosort version 2.5 was adapted to sort waveforms into clusters arising from individual motor units.
source: We therefore adapted Kilosort version 2.5 (Pachitariu et al., 2023; Steinmetz et al., 2021) and wrote custom MATLAB and Python code to sort waveforms into clusters arising from individual motor units (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–h).
evidence: This describes the spike-sorting software and modifications used for analysis.

claim: The spike-sorting code including modifications to Kilosort is available at https://github.com/JonathanAMichaels/PixelProcessingPipeline/releases/tag/v0.9.
source: Our spike-sorting code, which includes the above-mentioned modifications to Kilosort, is available at https://github.com/JonathanAMichaels/PixelProcessingPipeline/releases/tag/v0.9 (copy archived at Michaels, 2023).
evidence: This provides the location of the code repository for reproducibility.

claim: The close electrode spacing and proximity of contacts to muscle fibers in Myomatrix arrays ensure that each channel records from a much smaller volume of tissue than skin-surface arrays.
source: In Myomatrix arrays, the close electrode spacing and very close proximity of the contacts to muscle fibers ensure that each Myomatrix channel records from a much smaller volume of tissue than skin-surface arrays.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical design of the arrays.

claim: Myomatrix recordings include a smaller number of motor units represented on each recording channel compared to skin-surface recordings.
source: This difference in recording volume in turn creates different challenges for motor unit isolation: compared to skin-surface recordings, Myomatrix recordings include a smaller number of motor units represented on each recording channel, with individual motor units appearing on a smaller fraction of the sensors than typical in a skin-surface recording.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of the recording geometry.

claim: Skin-surface EMG analysis methods typically use source-separation approaches that assume each sensor receives input from most or all of the individual sources within the muscle.
source: Specifically, skin-surface EMG analysis methods typically use source-separation approaches that assume that each sensor receives input from most or all of the individual sources within the muscle as is presumably the case in the data.
evidence: This describes the analytical assumptions underlying skin-surface EMG analysis.

claim: The much sparser recordings from Myomatrix are better decomposed using methods like Kilosort, which are designed to extract waveforms that appear only on a small, spatially restricted subset of recording channels.
source: In contrast, the much sparser recordings from Myomatrix are better decomposed using methods like Kilosort, which are designed to extract waveforms that appear only on a small, spatially restricted subset of recording channels.
evidence: This is a methodological inference about the appropriate analysis approach for Myomatrix data.

claim: In over 100 Myomatrix injections performed in rhesus macaques, there were zero cases in which arrays broke such that electrode material was left behind in the recorded muscle.
source: Moreover, in over 100 Myomatrix injections performed in rhesus macaques, there were zero cases in which Myomatrix arrays broke such that electrode material was left behind in the recorded muscle, representing a substantial improvement over traditional fine-wire approaches, in which breakage of the bent wire tip regularly occurs (Loeb and Gans, 1986).
evidence: This is a quantitative safety measurement from the primate experiments.

claim: Breakage of the bent wire tip regularly occurs with traditional fine-wire EMG approaches.
source: Moreover, in over 100 Myomatrix injections performed in rhesus macaques, there were zero cases in which Myomatrix arrays broke such that electrode material was left behind in the recorded muscle, representing a substantial improvement over traditional fine-wire approaches, in which breakage of the bent wire tip regularly occurs (Loeb and Gans, 1986).
evidence: This is a known limitation of fine-wire EMG cited from prior literature.

claim: Insertion and removal of injectable Myomatrix devices appeared to be comparable or superior to traditional fine-wire EMG electrodes in terms of ease of injection, ease of removal, and animal comfort.
source: Insertion and removal of injectable Myomatrix devices appeared to be comparable or superior to traditional fine-wire EMG electrodes (in which a 'hook' is formed by bending back the uninsulated tip of the recording wire) in terms of ease of injection, ease of removal of both the cannula and the array itself, and animal comfort.
evidence: This is a qualitative assessment based on experimental experience.

claim: The songbird dataset shown in Figure 2g includes single-unit data from 8101 respiratory cycles collected over 74 minutes.
source: For example, the songbird dataset shown in Figure 2g includes single-unit data from 8101 respiratory cycles collected over 74 min, and, like the other acute recordings shown in Figure 2, recordings were ended by the experimenter rather than because of a loss of signal from individual motor units.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of recording duration in songbirds.

claim: Applying Myomatrix technology to human motor unit recordings will create novel opportunities to diagnose motor pathologies and quantify the effects of therapeutic interventions.
source: Applying Myomatrix technology to human motor unit recordings, particularly by using the minimally invasive injectable designs shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g and i, will create novel opportunities to diagnose motor pathologies and quantify the effects of therapeutic interventions in restoring motor function.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications.

claim: Myomatrix arrays might significantly reduce the risk and discomfort of clinical EMG procedures while also greatly increasing the accuracy with which human motor function can be quantified.
source: Moreover, because Myomatrix arrays are far more flexible than the rigid needles commonly used to record clinical EMG, our technology might significantly reduce the risk and discomfort of such procedures while also greatly increasing the accuracy with which human motor function can be quantified.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential clinical benefits based on material properties.

claim: The nervous system's control of skeletal motor output is ultimately mediated by motor units.
source: The nervous system's control of skeletal motor output is ultimately mediated by 'motor units,' each of which consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it activates, producing motor unit action potentials (Figure 1a) that generate muscle force to produce movement (Manuel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established neuroscience knowledge about motor control.

claim: A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it activates.
source: The nervous system's control of skeletal motor output is ultimately mediated by 'motor units,' each of which consists of a single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it activates, producing motor unit action potentials (Figure 1a) that generate muscle force to produce movement (Manuel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is the standard definition of a motor unit in neuroscience.

claim: Recent decades have seen tremendous advances in understanding the physiological mechanisms by which the brain controls complex motor behaviors.
source: Recent decades have seen tremendous advances in our understanding of the physiological mechanisms by which the brain controls complex motor behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Tools to record neural activity at scale have been critical to advances in understanding motor control.
source: Critical to these advances have been tools to record neural activity at scale (Steinmetz et al., 2018; Urai et al., 2022), which, when combined with novel algorithms for behavioral tracking (Machado et al., 2015; Berman et al., 2014; Pereira et al., 2019; Mathis et al., 2020; Wiltschko et al., 2020), can reveal how neural activity shapes behavior (Hernández et al., 2022; Vyas et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Current methods for observing the nervous system's motor output lag far behind neural recording technologies.
source: In contrast, current methods for observing the nervous system's motor output lag far behind neural recording technologies.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment of the state of the field that motivates the work.

claim: Traditional methods for recording muscle fiber activity via electromyography include fine wires inserted into muscles and electrode arrays placed on the surface of the skin.
source: Traditional methods for recording muscle fiber activity via electromyography (EMG) include fine wires inserted into muscles and electrode arrays placed on the surface of the skin (Loeb and Gans, 1986).
evidence: This describes standard EMG methods cited from prior literature.

claim: Surface electrode arrays are poorly tolerated by freely behaving animal subjects.
source: Moreover, fine-wire electrodes typically cannot detect single motor unit activity in small muscles, including the muscles of widely used model systems such as mice or songbirds (Pearson et al., 2005; Srivastava et al., 2015; Pack et al., 2023), and surface electrode arrays are poorly tolerated by freely behaving animal subjects.
evidence: This is a practical limitation of surface arrays based on experimental experience.

claim: High-resolution motor unit recordings have previously been achieved by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates.
source: Although this resolution has previously been achieved in moving subjects by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates (Hoffer et al., 1981; Robinson, 1970; Hyngstrom et al., 2007) and using fine-wire electrodes in moving insects (Pflüger and Burrows, 1978; Putney et al., 2023), both methods are extremely challenging and can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
evidence: This claim about prior methods is supported by citations to earlier work.

claim: Fine-wire electrodes have been used to achieve high-resolution motor unit recordings in moving insects.
source: Although this resolution has previously been achieved in moving subjects by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates (Hoffer et al., 1981; Robinson, 1970; Hyngstrom et al., 2007) and using fine-wire electrodes in moving insects (Pflüger and Burrows, 1978; Putney et al., 2023), both methods are extremely challenging and can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
evidence: This claim about prior methods is supported by citations to earlier work.

claim: Direct recording from motor neurons and fine-wire electrodes in insects are extremely challenging methods that can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
source: Although this resolution has previously been achieved in moving subjects by directly recording from motor neuron cell bodies in vertebrates (Hoffer et al., 1981; Robinson, 1970; Hyngstrom et al., 2007) and using fine-wire electrodes in moving insects (Pflüger and Burrows, 1978; Putney et al., 2023), both methods are extremely challenging and can only target a small subset of species and motor unit populations.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of prior methods.

claim: Combining high-resolution EMG with precise measurement of muscle length and force output will help untangle the complex relationship between neural control, body kinematics, and muscle force.
source: Of further interest will be combining high-resolution EMG with precise measurement of muscle length and force output to untangle the complex relationship between neural control, body kinematics, and muscle force that characterizes dynamic motor behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions.

claim: Combining Myomatrix recordings with high-density brain recordings or targeted manipulations of neural activity can reveal how central circuits shape motor activity.
source: Similarly, combining Myomatrix recordings with high-density brain recordings or targeted manipulations of neural activity can reveal how central circuits shape and reshape motor activity and – in contrast to the multiunit signals typically obtained from traditional EMG in animals – reveal how neural dynamics in cortical, subcortical, and spinal circuits shape the spiking patterns of individual motor neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications.

claim: The expansion of access to high-resolution EMG signals across muscle groups, species, and behaviors is the chief impact of the Myomatrix project.
source: This expansion of access to high-resolution EMG signals – across muscle groups, species, and behaviors – is the chief impact of the Myomatrix project.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the work.

claim: The microfabrication process consists of depositing and patterning a series of polymer and metal layers using spin coating, photolithography, etching, and evaporation processes.
source: The microfabrication process (schematized in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) consists of depositing and patterning a series of polymer (polyimide) and metal (gold) layers using a combination of spin coating, photolithography, etching, and evaporation processes, as described previously (Zia et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2022; Zia et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the fabrication methods with citations to prior work.

claim: The fabrication methods allow very fine pitch escape routing with less than 10 μm spacing between traces.
source: These methods allow very fine pitch escape routing (<10 µm spacing between the thin 'escape' traces connecting electrode contacts to the connector), spatial alignment between the multiple layers of polyimide and gold that constitute each device, and precise definition of 'via' pathways that connect different layers of the device.
evidence: This describes a technical capability of the fabrication process.

claim: Gold EMG recording electrode sites are formed by removing the top polyimide layer over each electrode site using reactive ion etching with O2 and SF6 plasma at a 5:1 ratio.
source: Once all the metal and polyimide layers have been deposited and patterned on carrier wafers, the gold EMG recording electrode sites are formed by removing the top polyimide layer over each electrode site using reactive ion etching process (O2 and SF6 plasma, 5:1 ratio).
evidence: This is a specific fabrication parameter.

claim: PEDOT:PSS was deposited on the electrode contacts to a thickness of 100 nm using spin coating.
source: PEDOT:PSS was deposited on the electrode contacts to a thickness of 100 nm using spin coating, resulting in final electrode impedances of 5 kOhm or less (100 × 200 um electrode sites).
evidence: This is a specific fabrication parameter.

claim: An Optec Femtosecond laser system was used to cut the electrode arrays into the desired shape/pattern.
source: Once all layers have been deposited on the carrier wafer, the wafer is transferred to an Optec Femtosecond laser system, which is used to cut the electrode arrays into the shape/pattern needed based on the target muscle group and animal species.
evidence: This describes a fabrication step.

claim: A Lambda flip-chip bonder was used to bond high-density connectors to the surface of the electrode array.
source: The final fabrication step is bonding a high-density connector (Omnetics, Inc) to the surface of the electrode array using a Lambda flip-chip bonder (Finetech, Inc).
evidence: This describes the final fabrication step.

claim: For chronic EMG recording in mice and rats, the array's connector was secured to the skull using dental cement.
source: For chronic EMG recording in mice and rats (Figures 1 and 2a, c, and d), arrays such as those shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–f were implanted by first making a midline incision (approximately 10 mm length) in the scalp of an anesthetized animal. The array's connector was then secured to the skull using dental cement (in some cases along with a headplate for later head-fixed chronic recordings), and the electrode array threads were routed subcutaneously to a location near the target muscle or muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This describes the surgical implantation procedure.

claim: For intramuscular implantation, a suture needle is passed through the target muscle and used to pull the attached array thread into the muscle.
source: For intramuscular implantation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h), a suture (size 6-0 to 11-0 depending on anatomical target) is tied to the distal-most suture hole. The needle is then passed through the target muscle and used to pull the attached array thread into the muscle.
evidence: This describes the intramuscular implantation procedure.

claim: The array is secured within the muscle by the passive action of the flexible polyimide barbs lining each thread and/or by adding additional sutures.
source: The array is then secured within the muscle by the passive action of the flexible polyimide 'barbs' lining each thread and/or by adding additional sutures to the proximal and distal suture holes.
evidence: This describes how the arrays are mechanically secured in tissue.

claim: A digitizing, multiplexing headstage was plugged into the connector and attached to data collection devices via a flexible tether.
source: For all Myomatrix array designs, a digitizing, multiplexing headstage (Intan, Inc) was plugged into the connector, which was cemented onto the skull for chronic applications and attached to data collection devices via a flexible tether, allowing EMG signals to be collected during behavior.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition setup.

claim: Data from the same 32 electrode channels on each Myomatrix array could be recorded either as 32 unipolar channels or as 16 bipolar channels by switching out different headstages.
source: By switching out different headstages, data from the same 32 electrode channels on each Myomatrix array could be recorded either as 32 unipolar channels or as 16 bipolar channels, where each bipolar signal is computed by subtracting the signals from physically adjacent electrode contacts.
evidence: This describes the flexibility of the recording configuration.

claim: Myomatrix signals were sampled at 30 or 40 kHz.
source: In all cases, Myomatrix signals (sampling rate 30 or 40 kHz) were first band-passed between 350 and 7000 Hz.
evidence: This is a data acquisition parameter.

claim: Individual motor units were identified from candidate units by assessing motor unit waveform consistency, SNR, and spike count.
source: Individual motor units were identified from 'candidate' units by assessing motor unit waveform consistency, SNR, and spike count, inspecting autocorrelograms to ensure that each identified units displayed an absolute refractory period of less than 1 ms, and examining cross-correlograms with other sorted units to ensure that each motor unit's waveforms were being captured by only one candidate unit.
evidence: This describes the quality control criteria for motor unit identification.

claim: Candidate units with inconsistent waveforms or more than 1% of inter-spike intervals above 1 ms were discarded.
source: Candidate units with inconsistent waveforms or >1% of inter-spike intervals above 1 ms were discarded.
evidence: This describes a quality control criterion for spike sorting.

claim: Candidate units with highly similar waveform shapes and cross-correlation peaks at lag zero were merged.
source: Candidate units with highly similar waveform shapes and cross-correlation peaks at lag zero were merged, resulting in sorted units with well-differentiated waveform shapes and firing patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e and f).
evidence: This describes a step in the spike-sorting process.

claim: DeepLabCut was used to track paw, limb, and body positions during mouse locomotion.
source: We used DeepLabCut (Mathis et al., 2018) to track paw, limb, and body positions.
evidence: This describes the behavioral tracking method with citation.

claim: Stance onset was defined as the time at which each paw contacts the ground and swing onset as the time when each paw leaves the ground.
source: These tracked points were used to identify the stride cycles of each limb, defining stance onset as the time at which each paw contacts the ground and swing onset as the time when each paw leaves the ground.
evidence: This defines the behavioral measurements used in the analysis.

claim: All procedures for mouse forelimb muscle recordings were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Emory University (IACUC protocol #201700359).
source: All procedures described below were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Emory University (IACUC protocol #201700359; data in Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) or were carried out in accordance with the European Union Directive 86/609/EEC and approved by the Champalimaud Centre for the Unknown Ethics Committee and the Portuguese Direção Geral de Veterinária (ref. no. 0421/000/000/2020; data in Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This is an ethical approval statement.
